Barney style breakdown of how the rules and scoring differ from traditional fantasy football:

The overall winner: The overall winner is whoever accumulates the most points throughout the playoffs by the end of the Super Bowl. There are no "games" or weekly opponents. You are trying to score the most total points throughout the playoffs.

No draft: Without a draft that means you can pick any players you like for your roster each week. Yes, that means you and other players will have some of the same guys on your team. There's an obvious strategic benefit to picking "sleepers" that you think will have a big game but aren't on many other rosters to break away from the pack in scoring.

Consecutive week starts multipliers. Each week in a row you start a player they earn a bonus multiplier for their score. For example if you start Aaron Rodgers in the wild card round you earn what he scores in the wild card round. If you start him a second week in a row in the divisional round during the divisional round his score is worth twice as many points to your total. If you start him again in the Conference Championship his score is worth 3x to your total for that game, and if you start him all four weeks of playoffs his Super Bowl points are worth four times to your total. Also just because you don't start a player in week one doesn't mean he can't earn a multiplier, just not as high. If you start Aaron Rodgers this week and the Packers lose, you of course will not be getting a consecutive week multiplier at QB for the divisional round. However, if you then start Cam Newton for the divisional round and the Pathers win Cam Newton is then eligible to score you a 2x multiplier if you choose to start him the NFC Championship game. Picking players that you think will not just score well but on teams who you think will advance is key.

Starting a player on their bye: You can start a player from a team on their bye week. They will earn a score of zero for you for the wildcard round. However, that does make them eligible for a consecutive week multiplier for you beginning in the divisional round. A player started on a bye then started in the divisional round will score twice as many points for you in that round and be eligible to continue racking up multipliers thereafter. In simple terms this means if you are confident a player is on a team that will make a deep playoff run and score a lot of points it may be in your best interests to take the goose egg in round one and start racking up bonus multipliers thereafter. It also means starting a player from a wildcard team is potentially worth the most points to you, since they will score in the first round whereas the bye-week layer will not. If you have a hunch a wildcard round team will make a deep run that is potentially the best scoring player you could choose. But if you don't have a feeling on any lower seeds but are sure a bye week team is Super Bowl bound you may want to back off and hope for that dangerous 4x Super Bowl multiplier.

Hopefully that spells out the differences in rules and scoring for any first timers. If anything is unclear post the question and we'll make sure everyone is on the same page.
